summary: A 100-ft CCC-era steel lookout at Pequot Lakes, MN, built 1935 and bought by Crow Wing County in 2018; open to the public to climb.

facts.design: Steel lookout tower, 100 ft tall, with a 7 x 7 ft enclosed cab about 9 ft high

access.note: Crow Wing County park; visitor guide says the tower is open to the public to climb

visit.trail_note: Park about one mile east of downtown Pequot Lakes with more than 3,000 feet of walking trails and interpretive signs

events.note: Current steel tower built by CCC labor, replacing a tower erected in late 1927; NHLR gives 1934
Retired DNR forester Keith Simar was manning the tower in May 2015 according to a news item
DNR sold the tower and about 40 acres to Crow Wing County for one dollar
County reported about $50,000 in repairs (stair treads, windows, guard rails, wire mesh) in October 2019

evidence.supports: built by CCC crews in 1934 (NHLR date)
evidence.quote: Minnesota’s second listing, Pequot Lookout Tower, was built by the CCC and MN-DNR Division of Forestry crews in 1934.
At 100’ with a 7x7 cab, it is still valued as a detection site in the popular wooded lakes region of central Minnesota.

evidence.supports: park named for former commissioner who preserved the tower
evidence.quote: named after a former Crow Wing County commissioner who spearheaded preservation of the tower.

evidence.supports: built by CCC in 1935 as a 100-ft steel tower
evidence.quote: an intact 100'-tall steel fire lookout tower built by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) in 1935

evidence.supports: current tower replaced the first tower using CCC labor
evidence.quote: In 1935 the agency replaced the first tower with the current tower using CCC labor.

evidence.supports: first lookout erected late 1927 and manned spring 1928
evidence.quote: The first tower was erected in late 1927 by the Minnesota Forest Service and first manned in the spring of 1928.
At the top of the tower is an enclosed cab that is 7' x 7' square and 9' tall.

evidence.supports: tower used for visitors rather than fire spotting about 2008-2014
evidence.quote: From approximately 2008-2014 the tower was not used for fire spotting but only for public visiting

evidence.supports: Simar started career as DNR forester nearly half a century before the 2019 MPR article
evidence.quote: He started his career here nearly a half century ago, as a forester with the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources.

evidence.supports: DNR stopped using and closed the tower several years before 2019
evidence.quote: The DNR stopped using the 85-year-old Pequot Lakes tower and closed it to the public several years ago because of safety and liability concerns.

evidence.supports: DNR sold tower and 40 acres to county for $1
evidence.quote: Last year, the DNR sold the structure — along with 40 acres of land — to Crow Wing County for $1.

evidence.supports: about $50,000 of repairs including stair treads, windows, guard rails and wire mesh
evidence.quote: The county made about $50,000 in repairs, installing new stair treads, windows, guard rails and protective wire mesh to prevent falls.

evidence.supports: retired DNR forester manning tower in 2015
evidence.quote: We travel up 100 feet to talk with Keith Simar, retired DNR forester who now mans the historical Pequot Lakes fire tower in search of fires.

evidence.supports: county acquired tower from DNR in 2018 for public reuse
evidence.quote: Crow Wing County acquired the tower and surrounding property from the Minnesota DNR in 2018

evidence.supports: park is a 40-acre county park with the tower open to climb
evidence.quote: The property features a historic fire tower open for the public to climb, more than 3,000 feet of walking trails
Today, visitors can climb the tower and take in a 20-mile bird’s-eye view of the surrounding landscape.
The centerpiece of the park is the Paul M. Thiede Fire Tower, built in 1935.

evidence.supports: park located about one mile east of downtown Pequot Lakes
evidence.quote: Located about one mile east of downtown Pequot Lakes, this 40-acre Crow Wing County park

corrections.why: The nomination's build history (CCC labor replacing a late-1927 tower) and the park's visitor guide both give 1935; NHLR's 1934 is not explained and is kept as a noted conflict.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR says 1934; the NRHP nomination and the county's visitor guide say 1935. The story follows the nomination's fuller history and notes the disagreement.

The nomination's photos date to 2014 and it says the tower was still in use for fire spotting; the 2019 MPR article says the DNR had stopped using it several years earlier. The story reports the later account as the current state and notes the 2015 news item.

notes_for_editor: Build year is disputed (1934 NHLR vs 1935 nomination and county). Current access comes from a 2026 visitor guide and was not checked on site. Staffing status rests on a 2019 article. The NRHP listing date was not confirmed.
